nodes.title: 4  drop name — once nothing uses it

meta.title: CI/CD & Deployments
meta.summary: Getting every change to production quickly and safely — and back out again just as quickly.

goals.text: Migrations that don’t break the old version

steps.title: Shipping by hand
steps.body:
Once a week, on Friday evening, a developer builds the app on their laptop, copies it to the production server over SSH and restarts it. Everyone stays late in case something breaks.

A week of everyone’s changes goes out at once — so when something does break, nobody is sure which change did it.

callout.text: Big, rare releases feel safer and are the opposite: the more that changes at once, the harder it is to test, to find the cause, and to undo.

steps.title: “It works on my machine”
steps.body:
This Friday the laptop had a newer library than the server, and the app won’t start. While the developer works out which of thirty changes to undo, the site is down.

There is no record of exactly what was running before, so even going back is guesswork. Four hours later, it’s up again.

callout.text: Builds that depend on someone’s machine, and deploys nobody can repeat exactly, turn every release into an experiment.

steps.title: Continuous integration
steps.body:
Now every push to the shared repository starts a [[pipeline]] on a clean machine: build the code, run the tests (see *Testing*). Nothing depends on anyone’s laptop.

The team merges small changes into `main` several times a day. A red pipeline means “stop and fix this first”, so `main` always builds and passes. That habit is [[continuous integration]].

callout.text: Keep the pipeline fast — ten minutes, not an hour. A slow pipeline makes people batch their changes again.

changes: + Shared repository, small changes to main
+ Every push: build + test on a clean machine

steps.title: Build once, promote the same artifact
steps.body:
The last stage packages the result into an **immutable artifact** — usually a container image — tagged with the commit it came from, `checkout:3f9c2a1`, and stores it in a registry.

That exact image is what gets tested, deployed to staging and then to production. Only configuration (addresses, secrets) differs between environments. What you tested is what you ship.

callout.text: Never rebuild for production: a rebuild can pull different dependencies and produce a different program from the one you tested.

changes: + Package stage: one image per commit

steps.title: Continuous delivery
steps.body:
Every image that passes is deployed to **staging** automatically — a small copy of production — where smoke tests check the main journeys. From there it can go to production at any time.

With [[continuous delivery]], production is one button press away. With continuous *deployment*, there is no button: every green change goes out by itself.

callout.text: Deploying daily makes each deploy small: a few changes, easy to review, easy to blame, easy to undo.

steps.title: Blue-green: switch, don’t replace
steps.body:
How does a new version reach users without downtime? With [[blue-green]] deployment there are two identical production groups. Blue serves everyone on v41 while v42 starts on green and warms up.

Then the load balancer switches all traffic to green at once. If anything looks wrong, switching back to blue takes seconds — it is still running, untouched.

callout.text: The cost is double capacity during a release. Rolling deploys (see *Load Balancing*) are cheaper but slower to undo.

changes: + Two production groups: blue (v41) and green (v42)
~ Load balancer switches all traffic to green

steps.title: Canary: try it on a few users first
steps.body:
A [[canary]] release sends a small slice of real traffic — here 5% — to the new version, and compares its error rate and latency with the old version’s (see *Observability*).

If v42 is worse, the pipeline rolls it back automatically and only a few users ever saw it. If it holds up, the slice grows: 25%, 50%, everyone.

callout.text: Canaries are testing in production — the only environment with real users, real data and real traffic patterns.

steps.title: Case: the migration that breaks the old version
steps.body:
v42 renames a column: `name` becomes `full_name`. The migration runs, and v42 is happy — but during the rollout most servers are still on v41, which asks for `name` and gets an error.

Fix it with [[expand and contract]]: add `full_name` and write both; backfill old rows; switch reads to `full_name`; only when no running version uses `name`, drop it. Every step works with both versions.

callout.text: During any deploy, old and new code run side by side against the same database. Every schema change must work with both.

changes: + Expand → migrate → contract, over several deploys

steps.title: Feature flags: deploy is not release
steps.body:
The new checkout page is merged and deployed weeks before launch — switched off. A [[feature flag]] decides, per request, who sees it: first the team, then 1% of users, then everyone.

Turning it off is a setting, not a deploy, so a problem is fixed in seconds. Deploying (moving code to servers) and releasing (showing it to users) become separate decisions.

callout.text: Flags are debt too: remove each one once its feature is fully out, or the code fills with branches nobody dares delete.

changes: ~ New checkout: on for staff + 1% of users

steps.title: Measure the delivery itself
steps.body:
Four numbers, known as the [[DORA metrics]], describe how well a team ships: how often it deploys, how long a change takes from commit to production, how many deploys cause a problem, and how quickly service is restored when one does.

Research across thousands of teams found the same thing this lesson shows: the teams that ship most often also break production least, because every change is small and every undo is fast.

callout.text: Speed and safety are not a trade-off here. Small, frequent, reversible changes improve both.

steps.title: Recap
steps.body:
• **CI**: small changes merged often; every push is built and tested on a clean machine.
• **Build once**: one immutable artifact per commit, promoted unchanged to every environment.
• **CD**: every green change can reach production at any time — by a click or automatically.
• Release carefully: **blue-green** to switch back fast, **canaries** to limit the damage, **flags** to separate deploy from release.
• Schema changes must work with **old and new code** at once: expand, then contract.

callout.text: That completes Shipping. Next module: **Whole Systems** — starting with how high-level and low-level design fit together.
